newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia's Hun Sen blasts Philippines, ASEAN.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's Hun Sen blasts Philippines, ASEAN.

text.p: Cambodian leader Hun Sen on Tuesday blasted Philippine President Fidel Ramos for meeting the country's ousted co-premier and warned his country would not join ASEAN if it had to wait until next year for membership.

Second Prime Minister Hun Sen said he was still interested in joining the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN), but that if membership was delayed until after the 1998 elections in Cambodia, he didn't want any part of the regional club.
"We are still ready (to join), but they have to tell us quickly in order to let us be ready to live alone or live with ASEAN," he said in a speech broadcast on national television.
"If I win the elections in 1998, I won't join ASEAN. Let ASEAN fail in its formula for Southeast Asia -- (seven) plus three without one," he added. "If we don't join ASEAN, we won't die."

ASEAN delayed Cambodia's membership in the wake of Hun Sen's July 6 power grab, when he ousted First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh. Cambodia had been scheduled to join the regional club along with Burma and Laos in late July.
Burma and Laos have now joined Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam in ASEAN.
Hun Sen also angrily criticised Ramos for meeting Ranariddh in Manila.
"(The Philippines) has far more problems than Cambodia," he said. "Don't interfere in Cambodian affairs."
Ousted First Prime Minister Ranariddh has been travelling throughout the ASEAN region to drum up diplomatic support, with Manila his latest stop.

On Monday Ramos reiterated the ASEAN position that all political forces, including Ranariddh, should be allowed to take part in national elections next year and called for a ceasefire in the northwest, where Ranariddh and Hun Sen's troops are still at war.
Philippine Lower House Speaker Jose de Venecia, who met Ranariddh on Tuesday, called on the Hun Sen government to agree to a compromise political settlement.
The statements apparently did not go down well with Hun Sen, who expressed anger that Manila received an "expelled" leader.
He said there had been coups in the history of the Philippines, adding "They should be aware of their own problems."
